title: What are Giants fans’ initial reflections on the 2026 season?
description: The season is over. Time for Giants fans to weigh in with their initial reflections on the season that was.
fullText:
The 2026 San Francisco Giants season is officially over. For better, and mostly worse. I'll have a lot more to say about this season as a whole in the coming days, as we all likely will, once the dust has settled.

But today, I wanted to check in and see what your initial reflections on this season are?

Personally, I feel relieved. I have loved this team since I was a child, and I have covered this team for 10 years and not one of those seasons has felt like such torture. On every front. Every part of this season has felt like misery to watch, write about, and I'm sure even to live for those involved in it.

So I am relieved. We are free of 2026 San Francisco Giants and I don't know that I've ever been happier for a season to come to an end. That's about all I've got at this point, so I'll hand the metaphorical mic over to you guys.

What are your initial reflections on the 2026 season?

title: Falcons Week 3, 3 up and 3 down: The offense shows signs of life
description: The offense was humming and CJ Henderson impressed in a big win.
fullText:
The Atlanta Falcons got their first win of the season, and did so in dominant fashion. Michael Penix Jr. returned, and so did the offensive production. On the other side of the ball, CJ Henderson and company stepped up as the team managed multiple injuries. Here's the Week 3, 3 up and 3 down.

What can't he do? Bijan Robinson is reaching heights no other Falcons running back before him has. In the first half, he became the 10th player in NFL history to reach 6,000 scrimmage yards before age 25. With Penix managing the game to near perfection, the heavy boxes started to disappear, allowing Bijan to stretch his legs. He finished with 213 total yards and two touchdowns. Robinson is on pace for +2,600 scrimmage yards, which would shatter the franchise record he set last year by 400 yards.

It had been 312 days since Penix Jr. set foot on the gridiron, and that showed during the 1st quarter. After shaking off the rust in the 1st quarter, the 3rd-year quarterback went 16/18 for 234 yards and a touchdown. It was how Penix accumulated these stats that has fans excited. Penix had a career high in both under center snaps and passes between the numbers, incinerating narratives from the Zac Robinson era.

He got his best friend Drake London involved, who has been disappointed by the Falcons start, to say the least. London was all smiles after putting up 194 yards, and so were Falcons fans. Penix's return has shifted the narrative around the team, and now we'll see what they are truly made of this season.

Henderson may not have had the career many envisioned as the first corner taken from his draft class, but he's rewriting his story in Atlanta. With A.J. Terrell on IR, Henderson needed to step up for Atlanta, and that's exactly what he did. He was the best defensive back on the field, forcing three incompletions and only giving up 40 yards on 11 targets.

He also had nine tackles on the day, showing he can handle his run support duties just fine. If these performances continue while Terrell is on the mend, the team will need to reevaluate if Mike Hughes is truly the best option as the team's second boundary corner on the depth chart.

Hell of a night for former top 10 pick CJ Henderson! #SFSP #ART pic.twitter.com/sxTDxlSC8N

The electric skill player is struggling to find a role and generate a spark. He had an extremely ill-advised punt return that left the team with worse field position than if he'd let it go, and outside of a handful of screens, he's a nonfactor in the offense. Rookies need time to acclimate to the NFL environment, so a slow start isn't cause for much concern, but his usage, regardless of whether or not he's getting the ball, is questionable.

Branch has the speed to stretch the field, and while he is smaller in stature, he can still function as a situational X receiver the same way Taylor Gabriel did for the offense almost a decade ago. We'll see if his role increases as both Jahan Dotson and Olamide Zaccheaus haven't done enough to justify their snap shares to this point.

When the Packers offense showed signs of life, Hughes was at the scene of the crime. He allowed five receptions on six targets for 89 yards and a touchdown. He also had a costly pass interference that flipped the field for the Packers offense. Hughes has been the target of Falcons fans' ire for a couple of seasons, and while sometimes the hate was extreme, there's no defending the quality of play we've seen in the opening window of the season.

Hughes' contract has always made the lapses in play easier to stomach, but with CJ Henderson coming on strong, it's getting harder and harder to justify his spot in this starting lineup. If he can't get it together over the next few weeks, he could find himself on the bench when Terrell returns.

Mike Hughes has been beat multiple times this season already. #Falcons pic.twitter.com/xXNVDYmNvJ

Pitts had a great block on Bijan Robinson's first rushing touchdown, and while his growth as a blocker has been needed, it isn't justifying his $53 million extension. When Kevin Stefanski was hired, his ability to get tight ends the ball was highlighted consistently. We still haven't seen that translate to the field. To be fair, this was the first game the team had a functional quarterback, so there's still plenty of time for his production to increase. If it doesn't, fans will once again start questioning his role on this team.

The Falcons needed this performance more than they needed air. Starting 0-3 would've been an early-season dagger the team and fans wouldn't have recovered from. They aren't out of the woods yet, sitting at 1-2, but new life has been injected into the season. The team has the opportunity to reach .500 after facing the Saints in Week 4 and get their playoff hopes back on track.

title: What do the numbers tell us about Hogh's Celtic start?
description: It is fair to say Kasper Hogh has not had the start he or Celtic would have wanted after the club spent a club-record fee to sign the Denmark striker from Bodo/Glimt.  Having bagged 53 goals in 102 appearances for his previous team, a handful of which came in the Champions League against top-level opposition, the 25-year-old arrived to fanfare following the signing of fellow big-money capture Camilo Duran.  Now, with Martin O'Neill's men on a three-game losing run, serious questions are starting to be asked after Hogh's underwhelming introduction.
fullText:
Nine games, three goals - and all three of those strikes coming in the one match.

It is fair to say Kasper Hogh has not had the start he or Celtic would have wanted after the club spent a club-record fee to sign the Denmark striker from Bodo/Glimt.

Having bagged 53 goals in 102 appearances for his previous team, a handful of which came in the Champions League against top-level opposition, the 25-year-old arrived to fanfare following the signing of fellow big-money capture Camilo Duran.

However, it is Duran who has hit the ground running while Hogh is yet to settle in the green and white after a challenging start to his Celtic career.

Anyone who wears the number nine shirt for the Parkhead club will always attract attention, and that is before you factor in a reported £11m transfer fee.

Now, with Martin O'Neill's men on a three-game losing run, serious questions are starting to be asked after Hogh's underwhelming introduction.

That said, three goals in seven starts is not an awful return, but all those goals came in the one outing against Kilmarnock in early August.

Hogh's hat-trick display that day sent an ominous warning to Celtic's domestic rivals, though he has not netted in seven fixtures since.

But what do the underlying numbers tell us? Do they paint a promising or more alarming picture?

A brief period out injured meant Hogh missed three league games for Celtic between the end of August and early September, but on a goals-per-90 basis the striker is second from top among all Scottish Premiership players with an average of 0.89.

Again, it should be noted that each of his three goals came in the 5-1 victory over Kilmarnock, but his expected goals per 90 (also 0.89) is the highest in the division.

A decent chunk of his total xG rating (2.99) also came in that rout at Rugby Park, but it has been performances elsewhere that have prompted concern, particularly in big games.

Hogh, along with Duran, was brought to Celtic with Champions League pedigree and with the hope of taking them to the next level in Europe, but he failed to score across both play-off legs with LASK and the Europa League opener with Ferencvaros.

In 109 minutes against Rangers this term, there has also been little involvement and no goal, although it would be unfair to pin that solely on the Danish forward.

Clear-cut chances have been few and far between in recent defeats for Celtic, with only two shots on target mustered in the Old Firm losses.

With the season threatening to unravel even at this early stage, O'Neill is yet to work out the formula to get the best out of Hogh, with Duran favoured through the middle from the start in the league defeat to Rangers last time out.

How the 74-year-old and his backroom team fit both into the attack could shape how their campaign unfolds, with a trip to Motherwell on the horizon.

title: Infrastructure of Dissent, Factionalism and the Battle for Accountability
description: A Peek Behind the Curtain: The Infrastructure of Dissent, Factionalism, and the Battle for Accountability. It’s the latest controversial column on Celtic Shorts by Colin Dempster…Colin DempsterRun...
fullText:
Running my engineering eye over the modern football club, it is clear that the machinery of power is heavily insulated by a sophisticated corporate communications apparatus.

Boardrooms operate behind clinical financial narratives, often supported by traditional media channels that prioritise institutional access over rigorous scrutiny.

However, beneath the official PR gloss lies a parallel, highly structured network of independent supporter organisations and alternative channels. As a fan media journalist for Celtic Shorts, Yahoo Sports, OneFootball, and LiveScore, I have watched and read countless hours of this ecosystem. To truly understand how modern football governance is challenged, one must look behind the curtain at the mechanics, divisions, and financial leverage of these grassroots movements.

The independent fan ecosystem is not a monolith; it is an interconnected network driven by distinct factions operating across the local and global landscape. Understanding who these groups are, how they coordinate, and the strategic choices they face reveals the true architecture of modern supporter activism.

The active resistance movement is built upon three distinct, operational pillars, each serving a unique function in challenging executive leadership:

Celtic fans banner marking poor European performances displayed by the Green Brigade. Celtic v Falkirk, Scottish Premiership, Celtic Park – 29 August 2026 Photo Stuart Wallace Shutterstock/IMAGO

The Match-day Vanguard: These are the collective groups located within the stadium standing sections. Operating without a centralised corporate hierarchy . Their focus is primarily cultural and visual—utilising large-scale tifo displays, coordinated vocal support, and match-day actions to preserve a traditional, working-class identity against hyper-commercialisation. Because their political expressions frequently clash with corporate compliance frameworks and regulatory bodies, they represent a persistent operational challenge for stadium executives.

Celtic v theRangers – Scottish Premiership – Celtic Supporters hold up a Let Celtic Flourish banner during the match at Celtic Park on Sunday September 1, 2024. Photo Steve Welsh

The Strategic Umbrella: This arm serves as the intellectual, boardroom-facing engine of the movement. Led by figures within the independent media landscape, this collective acts as a unified front to bypass traditional media blockages. Rather than relying solely on emotional matchday protests, this faction focuses heavily on corporate audits, data analysis, and structured campaigns designed to force institutional reform.

Celtic supporters at Celtic Park for the 2026 title showdown with Hearts. Celtic 3 Hearts 1. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

The Global Diaspora and Traditional Networks: Beyond the local stadium footprint lies a massive international network, including organised supporter hubs across Europe, North America, Canada, Ireland, Australia, the wider Australasian region, and the Middle East, alongside long-standing domestic travel associations.

Historically focused on matchday logistics and localised community hubs, these groups have increasingly aligned with the modern protest movement. For overseas supporters who rely entirely on digital streaming and independent channels to connect with the club, corporate stagnation and a perceived lack of sporting ambition are viewed as a direct failure of governance.

8th March 2026 Ibrox , Scottish Cup, Rangers versus Celtic. The Celtic Board in the main stand. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

The defining turning point of modern fan activism occurs when emotional frustration is translated into direct economic action. Recognising that executive boards frequently insulate themselves from verbal criticism, supporter collectives have developed sophisticated models of targeted financial disruption.

The premier example of this is the strategic implementation of targeted consumer boycotts. The design of these campaigns addresses a critical tactical question: How do supporters pressure a board without actively damaging the sporting integrity of the team on the pitch?

Guaranteed Stability: Supporters maintain their core commitments by continuing to purchase matchday tickets and renewing season registrations. This ensures the playing squad is fully insulated, matchday attendance remains at maximum capacity, and the club's essential revenue baseline is protected.

Targeted choking: Supporters systematically withhold all discretionary spending. This includes a synchronised refusal to purchase official retail merchandise, training wear, club-run stadium tours and food or beverages within the concourses on match days.

Hibs v Celtic, Easter Road, Scottish Premiership, 3 May 2026. Photo Photograph by Vagelis Georgariou

The real-world effect of this strategy is immediate and measurable. While essential ticketing revenue remains stable, high-margin retail pipelines and stadium operations suffer immediate drops. In highly synchronised campaigns, this selective starvation of optional revenue streams has successfully stripped away the commercial padding that executives use to justify static business models, forcing clubs to report distinct financial losses and bringing corporate complacency directly to light.

To understand how this infrastructure functions under pressure, one must look at the explicit operations carried out by different arms of the support and the exact changes they have forced upon the hierarchy:

The Radical Boycott Strategy: Matchday groups deployed immediate, targeted pressure by organising walkouts, enforcing complete stadium-kiosk blackouts, and refusing to purchase seasonal merchandise. Rather than merely venting on digital fan media comms, they transformed consumer spending into a literal blockade.

7th December 2025; Celtic Park,Celtic Fan Protest; photo Geo.

The Corporate Accountability Campaign: The strategic umbrella groups executed a highly organised commercial boycott designed to starve the executive suite of its optional corporate margin. They weaponised the financial data, successfully showing the broader support that compliance-driven business models were masking sporting stagnation.

The Shareholder and Legal Audits: Democratic cooperatives utilised small-scale shareholding power to directly confront the executive leadership within seasonal meetings. They stripped away performative focus groups, demanding independent fan representation, transparent ticketing operations, and an immediate end to executive nepotism.

The published year-end financial figures prove that this targeted economic disruption achieved immediate, undeniable results across the club's bottom line:

A multi-million retail plunge: While core ticketing revenue held completely steady at £49.1 million, the synchronised refusal to buy merchandise sent optional commercial and sponsorship income into a freefall, registering a £4.4 million drop, which is a 12% plunge.

Choking Stadium Profitability: By completely avoiding concourse food, beverages, programs, and luxury club tours, supporters delivered an immediate 25% hit to matchday stadium operations, shaving £2.7 million off corporate cash flows.

7th December 2025; Celtic Park, Celtic Fan Protest; photo Geo

Exposing the Corporate Alibi: This combined £7.1 million hit to optional spending tore down the boardroom's narrative of flawless business management. It forced the club to publish a £4.8 million post-tax financial loss, permanently stripping away the executive excuse that financial prudence justifies sporting stagnation.

For a long time, boardrooms have relied on a classic divide and conquer strategy to maintain their tight grip on power. Corporate PR teams and traditional media gatekeepers actively exploit the natural cracks in a fractured supporter base.

They deliberately paint match day ultras as an isolated fringe element, dismiss independent online forums as uncoordinated keyboard chatter, and treat long-distance diaspora networks merely as a passive revenue stream to be harvested for merchandise sales.

7th December 2025; Celtic Park, Celtic Fan Protest; Photo Geo

When the supporter movement remains fragmented, it plays directly into the hands of the executive suite. The everyday match-goer is left feeling deeply confused and alienated by different factions pulling in completely opposite directions.

One group calls for a stadium walkout, another asks for a peaceful protest, and a third defends the board's long-term financial caution. This tactical chaos creates an atmosphere of paralysis, allowing executives to completely ignore fan frustration because there is no single, authoritative voice holding them to account.

This is precisely why a complete amalgamation under a structured, democratic umbrella is the only true way to force institutional change.

Leaders should be voted in: True democratic legitimacy cannot be engineered from the top down or appointed behind closed doors. To maintain absolute accountability to the rank-and-file membership, the leaders of this unified front must be elected through direct, transparent voting processes open to every single member. Voting leaders in ensures that the executive command of the movement remains directly answerable to the people, preventing internal co-optation and keeping the strategic goals tightly aligned with the raw will of the supporter base.

7th December 2025; Celtic Park, : Celtic Fan Protest; photo Geo

A single, unavoidable financial weapon: Instead of disjointed, localised protests that only dent minor income pipelines, a massive, amalgamated front can coordinate economic campaigns globally. When supporters clubs, local stadium match-goers, and the entire international diaspora networks act as one single, disciplined block, they control millions of pounds in discretionary revenue. They can turn a regional dispute into a highly synchronised, devastating multi-million-pound hit to retail and stadium cash flows that forces the corporate executives to capitulate.

The power of legal and collective bargaining: A formalised, democratic collective carries the structural weight of a professional union. Because anyone across the globe can join, the movement completely smashes geographic boundaries, transforming a local stadium protest into a massive international block.

When representatives walk into operational meetings backed by a registered, voting membership that draws directly from a global fanbase of millions, they are no longer just individual internet commentators. They represent the literal lifeblood and the primary financial engine of the institution, forcing the hierarchy to negotiate on matters of ticketing, governance, and structural transparency with the same legal seriousness they would afford a major corporate partner.

Cutting through the noise: Most importantly, an amalgamated structure completely removes the confusion that paralyses the wider fanbase. It strips away the internal drama, the conflicting statements, and the factional infighting. It provides the ordinary, non-aligned supporter with a clear, transparent, and democratic portal to have their voice counted.

Dermot Desmond prior to the Celtic vs St Mirren Scottish Premiership match at Celtic Park on May 20, 2023. (Photo by Ian MacNicol/Getty Images)

The boardroom does not fear a fragmented fan media ecosystem trading arguments online. What terrifies the executive suite is an organised, intellectually unified support that refuses to be split by corporate spin. By trading fragmentation for democratic amalgamation, the fans build an institutional power that can directly challenge the boardroom, hold the leadership to account, and permanently shape the future direction of the club.

Despite measurable successes, a common counter-argument frequently surfaces within independent media spaces, typically driven by commentators who argue that consumer boycotts are ineffective. The core of this cynicism rests on a surface-level observation: The boardroom executives remain in office, the primary billionaire shareholders still hold ultimate equity control, and a localised drop in sales is dismissed as mere figures on a spreadsheet.

From this perspective, ordinary supporters are left wondering why they should make individual sacrifices—such as refusing to buy their children official replica jerseys or refraining from purchasing food at the stadium—when the structural leadership appears entirely unmoved.

This argument, however, highlights the exact psychological trap that keeps a corporate hierarchy in power. A professional boardroom relies heavily on the assumption that fans will prioritise immediate consumer convenience and tradition over long-term structural organisation.

7th December 2025; Celtic Park, Celtic Fan Protest; Photo Geo

When supporters act solely as uncoordinated individuals, buying merchandise and stadium food based on immediate personal desires, the board views this compliance as validation. A packed stadium store sends a direct message to executives that no matter how stagnant the product is on the pitch, the consumer base will keep funding the status quo.

Furthermore, dismissing financial deficits as just figures on a spreadsheet fundamentally misunderstands corporate anatomy. To a billionaire shareholder or a corporate executive, the spreadsheet is the only language that carries legal and operational meaning. They do not manage the club based on the emotional temperature of fan forums or phone-ins; they manage it based on balance sheets.

When a campaign forces a multi-million-pound commercial drop and triggers a significant post-tax loss, it strips away their executive cover, presenting an unvarnished audit to institutional banks, backers, and brand partners that corporate complacency is actively destroying the brand's equity.

To completely dismantle the board's defensive narrative, the unified movement must clearly define its true sporting objective. The boardroom's corporate PR machine consistently tries to misrepresent the protest, falsely claiming that dissenting fans are demanding reckless, unaligned hyper-inflation or asking the club to spend money it does not possess. This is a deliberate distortion.

Michael Nicholson, Chief Executive of Celtic and interim Chairman Brian Wilson arrives at the stadium before the Premier Sports Cup Quarter Final match between Rangers and Celtic at Ibrox Stadium on September 13, 2026. (Photo by Ian MacNicol/Getty Images)

The core vision of the collective mandate has never been about forcing the club to overspend above its organic means. It is not a call for fiscal irresponsibility, nor is it an emotional demand to run the business into catastrophic debt. Instead, the objective is centred entirely on a structural revolution: demanding that the club operate with far greater intelligence, sophistication, and modernisation across the entire football department.

A high-level engineering critique of the club's current model reveals an acute operational bottleneck. The problem isn't a lack of raw capital; it is a profound infrastructure deficit. While the boardroom hoards cash reserves and prioritises short-term balance sheet stability, the actual sporting engine—the recruitment structures, data analytics, global scouting tracking, and performance departments—has been left to rot.

The collective vision points directly to the club's European counterparts as a definitive proof of concept.

Across continental Europe, multiple clubs operating with identical revenue streams, matching turnover limitations, and similar domestic constraints consistently outperform our current setup on the European stage. They do not achieve this through reckless deficit spending; they achieve it by being fundamentally smarter.

They invest heavily in world-class sporting directors, build highly advanced algorithmic scouting networks, and create seamless, multi-club or data-driven player pathways that maximise the value of every single pound generated. By aligning the entire support around this exact blueprint, the movement proves that its goal is not economic vandalism, but elite structural evolution.

To translate this structural vision into a legal reality, the amalgamated movement must weaponise the single group of people capable of completely shattering the boardroom's defence: the traditional generation of supporters who built the club's financial bedrock.

These are the long-standing fans—frequently referred to as the traditional Celtic Da's—who stepped forward in early 1995 during the original stock exchange flotation to rescue the institution. Over 10,000 ordinary fans collectively answered the call, contributing millions and taking up an incredible 40% of the issued share capital at the time.

Fergus McCann Celtic director MD with model of new east Stand for Celtic Park

Over the last thirty years, through subsequent consolidations, share issues, and dilution, that ordinary individual fan ownership has settled at an explicit 17.5% of the club's entire registry, representing roughly 16.5 million shares split among approximately 27,700 individual small shareholders.

However, a staggering volume of those physical, paper share certificates are currently lying completely dormant—lost in old cupboards, tucked away in drawers, forgotten by families, or passed down to children who are entirely unaware of their legal value. Financial analysts estimate that up to 20% of the club's entire share registry is currently dormant or untraced.

Because a Public Limited Company is strictly governed by share percentages rather than individual head counts, unearthing this dormant capital is where the ultimate battle for accountability is won.

A crucial conversation must happen around family dinner tables globally to locate these forgotten papers. Supporter networks have a direct, professional pipeline to mobilise this hidden power through specialised corporate initiatives like Celtic Supporters Limited, fronted by financial expert David Low alongside business leaders Duncan Smillie and Peter McGowan.

This group specialises in tracing these lost holdings and coordinating proxy votes under a single, unified banner. The barrier has historically been a lack of corporate navigation; a member of the older generation knows he holds a certificate from 1995 but has zero desire to navigate stockbroker portals or track complex filings.

This is where the family conversation changes the game. The younger, digitally native generation must execute the heavy lifting: retrieve the physical certificate, identify the shareholder reference number, and contact the tracing vehicle.

Individual fans do not need to attend the AGM in person or face hostile floor mechanics to establish a significant say at boardroom level. By collecting these documents and legally appointing an amalgamated proxy, the fanbase stops acting merely as an external consumer protest.

It enters the annual general meeting as an undeniable corporate force. Legally assigning proxy votes directly to a unified vehicle instantly binds thousands of small holdings into a singular block of equity. Gaining control of even a fraction of that untraced 17.5% individual block completely changes the boardroom mathematics, turning dead capital inside a cupboard into an active corporate weapon capable of blocking director reappointments, halting unaligned restructuring, and forcing a direct seat at the table.

To measure the true impact of supporter activism, we must look past the superficial metrics of internet noise, short-lived stadium walkouts, or localised protests. Real, lasting impact is achieved only when separate, fragmented factions completely abandon their isolated identities and commit to total democratic amalgamation.

In the highly sophisticated arena of corporate football business, fragmentation is an absolute guarantee of defeat; complete structural consolidation is the only major winner capable of altering the balance of power. When a fanbase remains fractured into distinct subcultures, it operates as a collection of uncoordinated voices. The boardroom can safely isolate these individual factions, ignoring one while placating another with performative, hand-picked consultation boxes.

Complete amalgamation dismantles this defensive shield entirely. By building a formal, unified Supporter Union where every single participant holds an equal vote and leaders are transparently elected, the movement transforms from a loose protest network into a rigid, non-co-optable entity.

It establishes an undeniable democratic mandate representing the absolute lifeblood of the institution—a commercial and cultural force that corporate executives can neither patronise nor sweep under the rug.

This unified consolidation fundamentally alters how the fans fight the club, changing the battle from a series of emotional complaints into an unyielding economic siege. While fragmented groups trap the fanbase in internal drama and mass confusion, an amalgamated front provides absolute clarity to the ordinary supporter, allowing millions across the globe to act with synchronised discipline.

This collective leverage allows the support to step past the rigged voting system of Public Limited Companies and strike the boardroom directly in the commercial ledger. By concentrating their economic power into a singular, devastating multi-million-pound black hole, a unified fanbase strips away the corporate padding that shields executive complacency.

The ultimate achievement of this total mobilisation is not the destruction of the institution, but its forced modernisation. Underneath the temporary noise of boardroom friction and matchday frustration lies a profound, undeniable note of hope—a sentiment the fanbase needs right now more than ever.

The fanbase is no longer just waiting for permission to be heard, nor is it trapped in an endless loop of cynical, passive complaint. From the local streets surrounding the stadium to the far-reaching supporter clubs of Europe, North America, Canada, Ireland, the Middle East, and Australasia, a global community is actively building the blueprint for a modern, accountable, and transparent football club.

When the fans choose to look past the temporary exhaustion and speak through one single, unyielding democratic voice, the doom and gloom evaporates. It exposes a permanent reality that the boardroom cannot buy, spin, nor break: the future of this cultural institution belongs entirely to the people who love it.

title: Bellamy sure Wales belong as Haaland threat looms
description: Craig Bellamy expects Norway to be a force for years, but insists Wales have earned the right to be in Nations League A.
fullText:
Craig Bellamy remains convinced Wales are worthy of their place in the Nations League top tier despite a losing start to the campaign.

Wales are without a point in their group following a 2-0 defeat in Denmark just three days after losing 1-0 to Portugal in Lisbon.

Wales - without a victory in six matches in 2026 - have failed to win any of their eight matches in League A when combining their current efforts with those in 2022.

But having gained promotion from League B in his first campaign as boss, Bellamy insists Wales have earned the right to come up against Europe's elite on a consistent basis as they prepare to face Erling Haaland's Norway next.

"For us, this (Norway game) is another one, the intensity, top players, real speed," Bellamy added.

"It's what group A is, up and down all the group As. When we were in the pot, we were in pot four and we thought, 'where do you want to be?'.

"They're all brilliant, but we've earned the right to be here."

And Bellamy believes Stale Solbakken's men can be a force to be reckoned with for the coming years given the investment made in the national team.

"They get to the quarter-finals in the World Cup and you're really on a surge at the present moment," Bellamy said of Norway.

"This is a real surge now and I don't think it's going away.

"How rich your country is, it's really spending the money in certain areas and in sport, I expect you to be a force for a number of years."

While Bellamy was unbeaten in his first nine games after taking charge in July 2024, North Macedonia remain the highest ranked side - 65th - he has got the better of as Wales manager.

"I still want Craig Bellamy to be our manager, but I think there's an element of a new manager bounce when he first came in, there was an excitement and a freedom," former Wales international Nia Jones told the Feast of Football podcast.

"Sometimes the novelty wears off and expectations from opponents and fans go up, and I feel we've plateaued."

Wales now have two games to avoid going a full calendar year without winning for the first time since 1989, which would only put more pressure on Bellamy in his first international window since being linked with the Burnley job.

"When Craig took over, that first game against Turkey, the football was fantastic," said ex-Wales striker Nathan Blake.

"I remember our fans were like 'Wow, this is pretty, it's totally changed'. Everything was front-footed.

"Maybe the problem is because we were so good, on the front foot and the pressing was on point and catching teams off guard, maybe teams know what we're going to do."

Bellamy is not the only manager in the group under scrutiny and Denmark's victory over Wales helped to ease the pressure on boss Brian Riemer.

Three days after facing Norway at Cardiff City Stadium, Wales will take on Denmark once again.

Despite outclassing Wales in Copenhagen, Riemer said Bellamy's side should not be disheartened by their opening results in the Nations League.

"We have the utmost respect for Wales, they went through the B group without losing a game and were unlucky for the World Cup, they only went out on penalties.

"It is a team that has given a lot of teams problems. To go to Portugal and lose with just one is not something you should feel miserable about. We expect a very difficult game in Cardiff."

title: You are the Scotland boss - what would you change for Switzerland?
description: Put yourself in the shoes of the new Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli as he picks his first home XI to face Switzerland.
fullText:
Nations League: Scotland v Switzerland

Tuesday 29 September, 19:45 BST

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli takes charge of his first game at Hampden on Tuesday against Switzerland, live on the BBC, after an encouraging draw in his opening game away to Slovenia.

The Belgian chose eight uncapped players in his first squad with two of them - Robbie Ure and Stephen Welsh - making the starting XI in Ljubljana.

Ben Gannon-Doak and Kieron Bowie were the only substitutes used as Scotland dominated the second half but could not find a way to break the deadlock.

The Swiss represent a big step up in opposition, so will Pocognoli be tempted to tweak his team selection in Glasgow?

Scotland used three centre-backs on Saturday as Jack Hendry and Welsh flanked Scott McKenna.

Andy Robertson and Aaron Hickey were used as wing-backs, tasked with whipping crosses in for the attacking duo of Oli McBurnie and Ure.

There were some worrying signs in the opening 45 minutes in Slovenia as the hosts routinely stole in behind Scotland's high line.

However, it is unlikely the new boss will move away from his defensive strategy so early in his reign.

"We had a lot of good movement through the side, through the lines and we should have scored to be honest," he said after the goalless game.

"But the counter-press was good, the high [line] of the defence was good, just because the position of the players was better [in the second half].

"Clean sheet, that's also positive, but we want to win."

Uncapped pair Luis Binks and Luke Graham are the other centre-halves in the squad, so there's a good chance we see the same trio starting.

At the weekend, Gannon-Doak was introduced with just over 10 minutes and added menace to Scotland's attack.

Although he replaced Hickey, the Bournemouth winger is not an obvious fit at wing-back.

Might Pocognoli be tempted to use his searing pace up top rather than go with two strikers?

With four Nations League matches across 11 days in this window, utilising the squad will be key.

Hearts winger Josh McPake could also add a different dimension to the front line, after a bright start to the season for Hearts.

John McGinn started as a number 10 in Slovenia and was rather subdued but his experience, running power and goal threat make him such a key player for Scotland.

Billy Gilmour was the stand-out performer on Pocognoli's debut and really took the game by the scruff of the neck in the second half.

He was part of a double pivot with Serie A pal Lewis Ferguson but took up a more advanced role after the break, popping up regularly around the edge of the penalty box.

If there is to be a midfield change, Ryan Christie offers relentless energy and can fit in just about anywhere. Under Steve Clarke he did not get many chances in the middle of the park where he has done so well for Bournemouth.

Kieron Bowie, Robbie Ure and Oli McBurnie are the striker options, and all three are in good form and confident.

Ure and McBurnie are yet to score for their clubs this term, but both showed, in flashes, why they were given the starting nods by Pocognoli.

McBurnie, who dropped a little deeper after half-time, is the oldest and comfortably the most experienced of the trio but has yet to score after racking up 17 caps.

He should have done better with a chance against the imposing Jan Oblak, who pinched the ball off his feet.

Ure was described as "elegant" and showing "effortless" movement by pundit Pat Nevin during the game. He contested 18 duels in his time on the park - the most of any Scotland player.

He was determined to make an impact on his debut and went close to scoring with a strike that crashed off the post on the stroke of half time.

Off the bench with roughly 20 minutes to go, Bowie was a smart addition too, although the Sassuolo forward should have put Scotland ahead when he pulled an effort wide of the post.

The big question for the boss is do two of the three start against the Swiss, who were comfortable 3-0 winners in North Macedonia, or is there a need for speed or an extra man in midfield?

title: NI players relish Windsor return against Hungary
description: Northern Ireland's hosting of Hungary in the Uefa Nations League will be their first game in Belfast for 315 days.
fullText:
For the first time in 315 days, Northern Ireland are back in Belfast.

Michael O'Neill's side welcome Hungary to Windsor Park for a Nations League Group B2 contest on Monday night, just 51 days shy of a year since a Jamie Donley penalty saw the side to a 1-0 win over Luxembourg in their previous home fixture.

In the interim, they have played five times on their travels, a run that began with World Cup play-off defeat by Italy in Bergamo in March and concluded with victory over Georgia on Friday night.

If that win in Tbilisi represented a something of a breakthrough in terms of away performances - they had won just two of their previous 12 competitive away games - form back at Windsor has been strong despite the sporadic fixtures.

Since losing to Slovenia in October 2023, only Germany have left Belfast with a win and that a 1-0 triumph on a night the hosts missed numerous good chances.

A run of seven wins in nine home games is in stark contrast to what went before when, in the preceding nine at Windsor Park, Northern Ireland had beaten only San Marino and Kosovo, the latter courtesy of a 94th-minute winner.

O'Neill said he does not put much stock in such runs of form given the changing squads in international football, but acknowledged his team are in "a really good phase" at Windsor Park.

"This is a new team, so they're not saddled by the performance of previous teams," he said.

"They love playing here at the stadium. You know there was a period where the team of 2016 [who qualified for the European Championships of that year] didn't enjoy playing at home.

"Then suddenly they started to win games and they loved playing at home. Teams go through phases and at this moment in time this team is in a really good phase in terms of the home form."

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One NI, BBC Three, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary available online.

"I'm buzzing for it," said midfielder Patrick Kelly who has picked up four of his five caps on the road.

"Obviously, I made my debut there last year in November time and I haven't played there since, it's all been away games.

"We haven't been there in a while and I'm really looking forward to it."

For goalkeeper Pierce Charles, who saved a penalty from Khvicha Kvaratskhelia against Georgia, the wait to play again at Windsor has been even longer.

"Personally, I've not played there in over a year now and I can't wait to feel the place rocking. I just can't wait to see the fans and hear how loud it's going to be," said the 22-year-old whose last game in Belfast was June 2025 thanks to injury.

"I think we thrive off it. It just makes us excited, playing in front of a positive crowd, especially when we're doing well.

"They love to get behind us, which we all love, so it just drives us on to do better."

O'Neill left 'baffled' by refereeing in late win

Monday night is, however, not an average home fixture.

Northern Ireland take to the field around 73 hours after the final whistle in Georgia with the game in Tbilisi having required an almost 5,000-mile trip. Indeed, O'Neill noted that Monday night's hosts will have travelled further to get to Belfast than the visitors given that Hungary played Ukraine in Budapest on Friday.

To mitigate the impact of the travel, Northern Ireland players were kept on UK-time throughout the trip despite the three-hour time difference and flew through the night to make it back to Belfast on Saturday morning.

"The preparation between games is pretty much the same. The difficulty with this game was obviously we had quite a distance to travel - we've travelled further than the away team in this situation," said O'Neill.

"But that's the draw and that's the nature of how the fixtures came out but this is a good group. I think they'll be ready to play."

title: Yesterday sucked... I'll be back, says Cleary
description: Nathan Cleary responds to the horrific injury that has ruled him out of the Rugby League World Cup by promising "I'll be back."
fullText:
Nathan Cleary has responded to the horrific ankle injury that has ruled him out of the Rugby League World Cup by declaring "I'll be back."

The Australia great, 28, will miss the tournament in his home country after suffering a compound fracture and dislocation to his left ankle while playing for Penrith Panthers in their NRL play-off defeat by Newcastle Knights on Sunday.

Half-back Cleary - who helped Australia win the World Cup in Manchester four years ago - needed emergency surgery in hospital after being injured in a tackle by Phoenix Crossland.

Knights hooker Crossland was sent off for a 'hip-drop' tackle - which the NRL outlawed in 2020.

A hip-drop tackle is committed when a defender grabs the runner with both hands or wraps them with both arms, and then swivels or drops the hips or lower body, landing on and trapping the opponent's leg below the knees.

"Surgery done... Thank you so much to everyone that has reached out, the support has been unbelievable," Cleary posted on Instagram.

"Yesterday sucked but it's all part of the journey and it's made me even more grateful for the people I have around me. I'll be back."

Cleary had started Sunday's match on the bench because he was already carrying an injury to his right foot, which had a broken bone.

His father Ivan, the Panthers' head coach, said afterwards that his son would have surgery on both feet.

"I think that's why I was even more emotional on what happened to him, how hard he worked and what he put himself through to get himself to play today," the coach said.

Crossland was referred to the NRL Judiciary over the tackle, and is likely to receive a lengthy ban which would not only rule him out of Sunday's NRL Grand Final, in which Newcastle face Sydney Roosters, but may also affect his availability for New Zealand during the World Cup.

Australia will face New Zealand in the opening match of the World Cup in Sydney on 15 October (10:05 BST). The two teams are also favourites to face each other in the final, in Brisbane on 15 November (08:35 GMT).

title: FAI unclear over possible sanctions if game not played
description: Republic of Ireland could have faced "undetermined" sanctions had they not played their Nations League match against Israel on Sunday, according to FAI president Paul Cooke.
fullText:
Republic of Ireland could have faced "undetermined" sanctions had they not played their Nations League match against Israel on Sunday, according to FAI president Paul Cooke.

The players did not shake hands with each other and the Republic of Ireland squad bowed their heads when Israel's anthem was played before their 3-0 win in Hungary.

The two Nations League fixtures, being played at neutral venues, have been embroiled in controversy since February when the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.

The Republic of Ireland players have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace.

There was also no exchange of pennants between Republic of Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel skipper Manor Solomon, who did not shake hands.

Cooke added that along with standard punishments for not fulfilling a fixture, there was were also possible "undetermined" extras.

"No," he told RTE Sport when asked is Uefa threatened additional sanctions if one or both of the matches were not fulfilled.

"The rules are clear. It specifies if we don't fulfil the fixtures what the sanctions are and then there's reference to other sanctions undetermined.

"I think it depends on Uefa and what sanctions they levy on somebody as a result of it. We saw a recent thing in England and Southampton, the levies that were levied on them [expelled from the English Championship play-offs after admitting spying on opponents]."

Republic of Ireland 'raised awareness worldwide' in Israel game

Republic of Ireland defeat Israel in Debrecen

Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game

There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place with players locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding.

The FAI later confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game - the second match between the sides will take place on 4 October in the Serbian town of Backa Topola.

Cooke, who praised the players and manager Heimir Hallgrimsson after the victory, defended how the FAI dealt with the build-up to the controversial match.

"Some people think it was quite well handled.

"We said all along that we would play the game. That was mandated through us by our members, through the board, and we've fulfilled one of the fixtures now thanks to the courage of those players who played tonight and togged out."

Cooke was also asked about Uefa's response to an FAI letter sent last November which proposed Israel's expulsion from international and club competitions.

"Their response was that they'd consider it and they're still considering it," he said.

Cooke has spoken to the the two other countries in the group - Austria and Kosovo - asking if would they back sanctions against Israel.

"I've certainly spoken to the other countries in our group and they reaffirmed their decisions to play the games."

title: Olympic champion Marchant retires from cycling
description: British Olympic gold medallist Katy Marchant says it has not been a difficult decision to quit the sport.
fullText:
Olympic gold medallist Katy Marchant has announced her retirement from cycling.

The 33-year-old helped the women's team sprint trio win Britain's first Olympic gold in that event at the 2024 Paris Games.

In the same year, she won World and European titles, to add to an individual sprint bronze medal on her Olympic debut in Rio in 2016.

Marchant said she considered continuing to the next Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028 but her 13-year career came to an end with a silver at this summer's Commonwealth Games.

"I've achieved more than I could ever have dreamed of achieving," said Marchant.

"It feels really strange. It's not been a difficult decision.

"Don't get me wrong, there have been moments where I've thought, 'could I just, should I just, what if I just?' But I know what it takes to push on for another two years.

"I'm incredibly proud of where I've got to and what I've done.

"I just don't want to make those choices anymore to keep doing what it takes to get to LA."

Marchant was a British junior heptathlete who was persuaded to switch to cycling in 2013 after a coach noticed her impressive times on a static bike.

In 2024, Leeds-born Marchant became the first track sprinter to return to elite competition after becoming a mum. Two years after the birth of her first child, Marchant won Olympic, World and European titles before a crash which required operations on her arm and kept her out of racing for 12 months.

She returned to the track again in January this year, six months after the birth of her second child, then won Commonwealth silver in the team sprint with Rhianna Parris-Smith and Sophie Capewell in July.

In the lead-up to the Games, Marchant spoke of her goal to compete at LA 2028, but has now told BBC Breakfast that she is instead looking forward to "a little bit of freedom".

"I'm actually enjoying the time at the minute to be able to reflect on my journey - something we don't do enough when we're in it," she said.

"I'm a farmer's wife, so there could be a bit of that. I have a small cake business that could grow, there is potential. And I'm addicted to high performance and I absolutely love sports. So that might be my path going forward. But I really, really don't know."

"I had a good work-life balance, but I've been enjoying not having to focus on the amount of protein you're eating every day. I'm feeling a little bit freer.

"I've been able to do the school drop-offs, been able to do the swimming lessons, things like that, things that I haven't massively been able to do so much.

"I'm really enjoying just being me."

title: Broncos deny Rams and Seahawks lose - five things from NFL week three
description: The NFL produced another thrilling day of action with a shock for the defending Super Bowl champions and several tight finishes.
fullText:
The NFL produced another thrilling day of action on Sunday with a shock for the defending champions as five teams maintained their unbeaten record this season.

There were several nail-biting finishes as 12 of the 14 games were decided by eight points or fewer, tying the NFL record for the most one-score games in a day.

One of those took place in Brazil, where the NFL staged the second of a record nine international games to be played this season.

But they saved the best for last as the two teams that went within one win of last season's Super Bowl traded blows in a gripping primetime clash.

The Denver Broncos and the Los Angeles Rams remain potential Super Bowl contenders after losing last season's Conference Championship games.

Both teams had an underwhelming season opener before bouncing back last week, and Sunday's game in Denver gave them an opportunity to show their title credentials.

The Rams dominated the first half and led 16-0 at the interval, but the Broncos regrouped to draw level in the third quarter.

That set up a fascinating finish, with three lead changes in the final five minutes, beginning with an interception by Denver safety Talanoa Hufanga which he ran back for a 66-yard touchdown.

In just over a minute, last season's Most Valuable Player Matt Stafford led the Rams down the field, culminating in a 48-yard touchdown for receiver Konata Mumpfield to regain the lead.

The Broncos replied with quarterback Bo Nix reaching into the endzone after another long drive to put the hosts back in front.

That left Stafford 47 seconds to get into a game-winning position and he did just that. With two seconds left, he had a shot at the endzone from 19 yards, but Hufanga intercepted for a second time to clinch a 30-26 Broncos win.

The Washington Commanders' hopes of getting back in the play-offs were dealt a huge blow last week as quarterback Jayden Daniels dislocated his left elbow.

But Daniels could be back inside three weeks and, although the Commanders hosted defending champions the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday, they led 24-10 after experienced back-up Marcus Mariota threw his third touchdown pass.

The Seahawks drew level in the fourth quarter, but Sam Darnold, who returned from a game out for Seattle, then threw his second interception, and it was returned by linebacker Kain Medrano for a 50-yard score.

That proved enough for Washington to clinch a 33-31 win and halt a 12-game win streak by Seattle, which included last season's Super Bowl run.

The New England Patriots were their opponents in the Super Bowl, but their quarterback Drake Maye has struggled since.

After having only 11 turnovers last year, he already has seven this season after another three against the Jacksonville Jaguars, and he was benched as the Jags romped to a 35-6 home win.

After playing in Sao Paulo the past two seasons, the NFL returned to Brazil for its first game in Rio de Janeiro.

There had been concerns about the condition of the field at the iconic Maracana stadium, but there were no issues.

The NFL picked a mouth-watering match-up for Rio and it delivered, with the Baltimore Ravens and the Dallas Cowboys producing a thriller.

Two Derrick Henry touchdowns helped the Ravens into a 24-13 lead in the third quarter before Dallas, playing only their second international game, fought back.

The lead changed hands twice in the fourth quarter and the game looked set for overtime when a Cowboys field goal levelled the score with seven seconds left.

But Lamar Jackson then completed a 27-yard pass down the middle to get the Ravens within field-goal range and Tyler Loop made a 56-yard kick as time expired to win the game 34-31.

That sparked wild celebrations at the Maracana and means all four AFC North teams have a 2-1 record this season.

Some Cleveland Browns fans cheered when quarterback Deshaun Watson suffered a season-ending injury in 2024.

Some booed as he returned to action in pre-season, but could Watson finally be winning over the 'Dawg Pound'?

The 31-year-old led the Browns to a comeback win at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last week and repeated the feat as Cleveland beat the Carolina Panthers 21-18 in their home opener.

Watson held his nerve to step out of the pocket and fire a 14-yard touchdown pass to tight end Harold Fannin Jr to cap a game-winning 65-yard drive.

"The past is the past," said Watson. "I know we've been through some ups and downs. But if we look forward, build off this win, come back Thursday night and get another big one, we can make something special for this city."

The Browns are at home again on Thursday against divisional rivals the Pittsburgh Steelers, who enjoyed a morale-boosting victory in another AFC North match-up on Sunday.

After only one offensive touchdown in their opening two games, Aaron Rodgers got the Steelers firing, throwing three touchdown passes before Derrick Harmon pulled off a strip-sack on Joe Burrow to seal a 30-27 win at home to the Cincinnati Bengals.

Three of the teams who remain unbeaten are regular play-off contenders. The Buffalo Bills came from 10-0 down to beat the Los Angeles Chargers 24-16, with quarterback Josh Allen barging over for two touchdowns.

Travis Kelce scored as the Kansas City Chiefs won 24-10 at the Miami Dolphins, while Brock Purdy threw four touchdown passes in the San Francisco 49ers' 36-30 win at home to the Arizona Cardinals.

Few expected the Minnesota Vikings to be 3-0, though. They won 23-16 at Tampa Bay despite losing receiver Justin Jefferson to an early ankle injury.

And the biggest surprise has been the Las Vegas Raiders. They have now won as many games as they did last season, when they had the league's worst record.

For the third straight game veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins threw for three touchdowns as the Raiders fought back from 27-16 down to win 35-27 at the New Orleans Saints.

The Philadelphia Eagles could make it six teams with a 3-0 record when they end week three with a trip to the Chicago Bears on Monday.

title: Is Premier League possession football on the way out?
description: Only 36% of teams with more than 60% possession have won this season in the Premier League. BBC Sport looks at why?
fullText:
In the early 2000s, Premier League defences tried to make the pitch as small as possible, giving their opposition less space to score in.

Coaches therefore encouraged their attackers to play quickly, taking advantage of open space that saw them face fewer defenders.

Logically, this made total sense.

It was Pep Guardiola's influence that, in part, flipped this logic on its head over the last decade.

His Manchester City sides looked to force teams back into a compact defence, a challenge that in theory should be harder to break down.

The counter logic was that they were forcing opponents to give them a familiar challenge they were prepared for.

City's defenders also had big spaces to cover, often standing at the halfway line.

But for Guardiola, those spaces were less worrying if the ball stayed near the opposition's goal for as long as possible.

After all, if you have the ball, the opposition cannot score.

So why now are teams that dominate the ball dropping points?

Across this season's opening 50 Premier League matches, teams recording at least 60% possession have won only 36.4% of those games, while in 2023-24, the figure was 53.5%.

Does this suggest possession football is on the way out? Well, the answer isn't that simple.

Are teams winning because of their low possession, or having less possession because they have taken the lead early?

There could be some truth in both answers.

Let's use Xabi Alonso's Chelsea as a case study.

They won their opening games against Fulham and Brighton - 3-2 and 4-3 respectively - with the minority of possession, then drew 2-2 with Hull and lost 3-0 to Brentford despite having considerably more of the ball.

Against Brighton, Chelsea's 25.6% possession and 146 successful passes were their lowest recorded figures in a Premier League match, with records beginning in 2003-04.

And yet, the Blues scored four goals.

For three of them, accelerating play from throw-ins and counter-attacks allowed their direct attackers to find space against fewer defenders.

This dynamic can partly be explained by Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton wanting to dominate the ball - with only Manchester City averaging more possession than the Seagulls this season - which played into Chelsea's hands.

Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto and Morgan Rogers boast skillsets suited to transition-heavy football, and the low possession against Brighton helped them play to their strengths.

Counter-attacking comes with a stigma.

It is more accepted underdogs like newly promoted Hull will play this way. For bigger teams, there is an expectation to eventually control the game with the ball.

This makes a low-possession approach harder to sell long term, even if the players might look better conceding possession.

And that disconnect between players' skillsets and tactics could help explain some dropped points.

Alongside Chelsea, Manchester United have also suffered in this way. Under Michael Carrick, they have averaged 1.5 points per game with more than 50% possession. With less, that rises to 2.6.

Clubs without the same expectation, like Brentford, Leeds and Hull, can concede possession and have built squads for that style.

With impressive box defenders, dangerous counter-attackers and set-piece specialists, their tactics can align with their players' strengths, helping them compete against more less aligned opponents, irrespective of their wealth gap.

In recent seasons, there has been a rise in man-to-man pressure that has made building out from the back challenging.

Teams, as a result, have looked to play long over the press or past its first line into space for players to drive with the ball - think the likes of City's Nico O'Reilly or Arsenal's Declan Rice.

Both of these have been great solutions to the initial problem, but it does mean that teams full of physical athletes, focused on bringing down long passes or driving with the ball over distance, could be less suited to the intricate play required to unlock stubborn defences - a situation commonly faced by teams who have more of the ball.

To dominate in 2026 likely requires a squad that has enough solutions in small spaces as well as big ones.

Opponents have used man-to-man defending closer to goal too, making it harder to find the unmarked player, a key attacking principle used in Guardiola's positional play.

With players marked, attacks can then depend on winning one-against-one situations, requiring individual quality often in the form of dribbling.

Given the way teams have been built over the last few years, certain sides may lack this type of problem solver.

It is important to note possession is an average across a match, which can hide how the scoreline changes a team's approach.

Chelsea scored within seven minutes in each of their opening four league games after which opponents pushed forward looking for a goal. The Blues dropped deeper, defending their lead and attacking the space left behind.

Across their opening five matches, Chelsea averaged 51.4% possession when level, 34.5% when ahead and 67.2% when behind - highlighting how much their possession has varied with the score.

Interestingly, protecting a lead created favourable opportunities for Chelsea's attackers to play intuitively, carry the ball and attack space. When chasing a goal, they had more possession but appeared to lack solutions against compact defences.

Arsenal show the value of being able to do both parts well when needed.

Bukayo Saka and Max Dowman's dribbling, combined with the passing of Martin Odegaard, Martin Zubimendi, Bruno Guimaraes and Christos Tzolis, provides repeatable solutions against packed defences.

Their set-piece threat can also give them the lead when clear chances are difficult to create despite dominating the ball.

Once ahead, Arsenal's possession falls from 60.4% to 56.6% - a small drop but a signal of intent.

Gabriel, Ezri Konsa, Jurrien Timber and Rice then offer the defensive quality to control the game with less of the ball.

Manchester City protect leads differently. Their possession remains at 64.9% when ahead. This approach works partly because it is familiar to the squad Enzo Maresca inherited from Guardiola in the summer.

Rather than repeatedly defending their penalty area, they protect their advantage by keeping the ball and keeping opponents away from their goal given their technical quality.

From all of the successful examples, the same objective is being achieved: a game that suits your players and one that makes the opposing players uncomfortable.

"If you are brave, they have to play a game that is not [the opponent's] preferred game," current Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola told The Independent in 2025.

At the time, he was managing Bournemouth - a team notorious for winning with less of the ball against some of the league's best.

It would be fair to argue fewer teams in the league now have the players or the solutions needed to break down teams given the evolution in defensive tactics, and advantages are more commonly found in attacking the big spaces.

Therefore bridging that gap, from thriving without the ball to dominating with it, will take time for those wanting to do so.

But at the top level, this is time not all coaches are afforded.

Lando Norris has apologised to Franco Colapinto for saying the Argentine should be banned for causing an accident at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Colapinto locked up at the restart after a safety-car period and slid into Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly, who then hit McLaren driver Norris, in an incident which resulted in all three retiring from the race.

Colapinto said he was "sorry" for his "big mistake" but Norris, speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, said: "Give him a ban. It's quite simple."

In a message on Instagram, world champion Norris said he was sorry for his comments on Saturday.

"Tough weekend overall in Baku and of course a disappointing and early end to the race," he said.

"Me and Franco came to a good understanding, are still good friends and are both excited to get back racing this weekend."

title: A 31-year wait for success - but can Everton fans still celebrate?
description: Is supporting Everton a life of misery, or are there still reasons to celebrate? Chief football writer Phil McNulty seeks the answer.
fullText:
Everton's unbeaten start to the Premier League season and progress in the Carabao Cup has prompted a minor outbreak of something rarely felt among their fanbase in recent times - optimism.

Guarded optimism, understandably, but the mood has shifted somewhat since the fury that followed a badly botched transfer window, typified by a shambolic final day that left manager David Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players.

A move for AS Monaco striker Falorin Balogun fell through when he walked away from the deal after problems with the medical, while Iliman Ndiaye, arguably Everton's best player, was sold to Manchester City for £65m.

It is against this backdrop that Moyes seeks to end Everton's 31-year search for success that has saddled them with an unwanted record.

Since the turn of the century, Everton are the only club in English football's current top four tiers who have not won a trophy - their last being the 1995 FA Cup triumph against Manchester United at the old Wembley - or been promoted.

Of course, to the enjoy the rush of promotion, Everton would first have to suffer the pain of relegation.

It nearly happened this millennium as Everton - last relegated in 1951 - stayed up by beating Bournemouth on the final day of the 2022-23 season. They had only guaranteed safety in the previous campaign by coming from two goals down to beat Crystal Palace in their penultimate game on a night of thunderous sporting theatre at Goodison Park.

So is supporting Everton a life of unrelenting sporting misery? Or is there still joy and celebration to be had following of one the grand old English football institutions?

Former player Leon Osman, who made 433 appearances for Everton between 2003 and 2016, scoring 58 goals, says: "Yes, there have been disappointments and those years without trophies, but let me tell you this - I wouldn't swap being an Evertonian for anything in the world."

And prominent Everton fan Dr. David France, who calculates he has travelled two million miles - the equivalent of going to the moon and back four times - to watch his beloved club from his home in the United States, told BBC Sport: "I can explain what I celebrate, even if we haven't had tangible success for so long. I celebrate being an Evertonian."

Others who also celebrate supporting Everton include Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canada counterpart Mark Carney, who recently both attended the 1-0 EFL Cup win against Wolverhampton Wanderers at Hill Dickinson Stadium that set up a last-16 home tie with Newcastle United.

Moyes demands more from Everton - but don't mention Europe

The statistics that pile pain on Everton and their fans reflect those occasional highs and more regular lows - but always accompanied by fiercely passionate, loyal support and sold-out games, at Goodison Park and the magnificent new Hill Dickinson Stadium.

And Everton remain one of only six Premier League originals, along with Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur, who have never dropped out of the top tier.

Elsewhere, Everton's tale of the tape is not so flattering.

Since 2000, they have lost two FA Cup semi-finals, winning a third against Manchester United on penalties in 2009, only to lose to Chelsea in the final.

Everton have been knocked out eight times at the first time of asking in the third round.

In the EFL Cup, they have only reached the semi-finals twice, in 2008 and 2016, losing both.

In the league since 2000, Everton have failed to win at Chelsea in 27 attempts, won only twice at Manchester United, once at Arsenal and Liverpool and five times at Manchester City. Everton did win an FA Cup fourth-round replay at Stamford Bridge in 2011.

In the 53 Merseyside derbies in the Premier League in this time, Everton have won only five and lost 28.

Their ledger is balanced by a dramatic FA Cup fourth-round replay win against Liverpool in 2009, secured with Dan Gosling's last-minute goal in extra-time, as well as a crucial 1-0 derby win that was part of their finest season in this fallow period.

In 2004-05, Everton manager David Moyes performed what then Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger described as "a miracle" when, after selling Wayne Rooney to Manchester United, he guided them to fourth place and into the Champions League.

It was a campaign that contained another of Everton's celebratory moments, when Duncan Ferguson tormented Sir Alex Ferguson's Manchester United, scoring the winner with a trademark header from Mikel Arteta's free-kick on another memorable Goodison night.

Sadly, Everton's journey into the Champions League qualifying round ended in heartbreak and controversy when, after losing the first leg 2-1 at home to eventual semi-finalists Villarreal, referee Pierluigi Collina mysteriously ruled out a late Ferguson header that would have sent the tie into extra-time.

They eventually went out 4-2 on aggregate following a decision that still rankles today.

So is it really as bad as all that?

Osman is well qualified to answer, having enjoyed a distinguished first-team career at Everton stretching between 2003 and 2016.

He told BBC Sport: "We've had some disappointments in those times, certainly in terms of not winning anything, but we've had some good days along the way, good moments.

"We've reached semi-finals, an FA Cup final, some great celebrations. We had some great trips in Europe - I think about us winning in Nuremberg in the Uefa Cup with thousands of our fans there to enjoy it.

"I certainly don't feel it's been 26 years of misery. I would argue very strongly against that. When we qualified for the Champions League in 2005, that was an incredible achievement, given the clubs we were up against. We did something very special in that season."

Osman added: "I am more than upset than any Evertonian in the world that we haven't won anything in the last 20-30 years, certainly in the period I played when I could affect it, but there has never been a single moment when I would swap being an Evertonian for anyone else.

"It's better to be an Evertonian than to support any other club, and you mark my words, if and when we do get silverware, just you watch those celebrations. They will be something else."

The fan's verdict comes from Dr. France, whose devotion to Everton can be measured in those two million miles.

This is the result of countless transatlantic trips the 78-year-old has made from Arizona in the United States, the country which has been his base since 1977.

Dr. France is no ordinary Everton fan, attending his first game on 4 September 1957 when Everton drew 3-3 with Manchester United's Busby Babes.

He established the Everton Former Players' Foundation in 1999, and is the club's premier archivist, with more than 20,000 items of memorabilia, which he transferred into public ownership via The Everton Collection Charitable Trust and is now maintained at the Liverpool Record Office.

"I think we missed the boat after the Premier League ship sailed. We are no longer the best of the rest," Dr. France acknowledges.

"For about a 10-year period under David Moyes we averaged about sixth or seventh and we had the odd hard-luck story, and more recently for a three-year period we could almost be described as a laughing stock. Hopefully that's no longer the case.

"We aren't with the Aston Villas and the Newcastles, who are challenging for the best of the rest, but we live in hope."

And how much has his devotion to Everton cost him?

"A robust seven-figure Littlewoods Pools jackpot," he says in a nod to the company formed by Everton's patriarch of the 1960s and 1970s Sir John Moores, whose vast fortune earned the club the nickname 'The Mersey Millionaires'.

"If I'm picking one recent celebration at a game," says Dr. France, "it would be our 2-0 win over Liverpool at Goodison in April 2024 - our first win in 30 derbies, excluding the 2-0 win behind closed doors at Anfield [during the Covid-19 pandemic].

"I was sitting in the second row of the directors' box and three rows behind me was a certain Andy Burnham, fists clenched and punching the Merseyside air.

"I'm very lucky to be part of something very special supporting Everton. It is a special community. You don't become an Evertonian to be a glory hunter do you?

"We have loyalty inbred into us. We don't just support the club, Evertonians support one another. We are a family. When I go to watch Everton, I feel like I'm among friends."

And he hopes he and those fellow Everton fans will have something to celebrate soon.
